## Introduction

Emily Dickinson wrote short poems about broad subjects and used dashes frequently (`--`).
I used string functions and regular expressions to ask:

1. Which themes (death, love, nature, God) show up most often in her poems?
2. Does her use of dashes differ across the three groups of poem files in the data?

## Data source

* **R package:** `DickinsonPoems` by Nicholas Horton, available at
  <https://github.com/Amherst-Statistics/DickinsonPoems> and installed with
  `devtools::install_github("Amherst-Statistics/DickinsonPoems")`.
* **Original source:** the Project Gutenberg edition of Emily Dickinson's poems,
  <https://www.gutenberg.org/files/12242/12242-h/12242-h.htm>.
* Each poem is stored as its own text file (like `gutenberg1.txt001`). I call the digit
  after "gutenberg" the "file group" (1, 2, or 3).

## Reading in the data

The regular expression `(?<=gutenberg)\\d` uses a **lookbehind**
to grab the digit that comes right after "gutenberg" in the file name.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(DickinsonPoems)

poems <- tibble(file = list_poems()) |>
  mutate(
    text = map_chr(file, \(f) str_flatten(get_poem(f), collapse = "\n")),
    group = str_c("File group ", str_extract(file, "(?<=gutenberg)\\d")),
    n_dashes = str_count(text, "--")
  )

head(poems)
```

## Question 1: Which themes show up most?

For each theme I wrote a regular expression of related words. `(?i)` makes it ignore
capital letters, and `\\b` marks a word boundary so that "die" does not match inside a
longer word. `str_detect()` checks whether each poem contains a match, and the average
of those TRUE/FALSE values is the share of poems with that theme.

```{r}
themes <- poems |>
  summarise(
    Death = mean(str_detect(text, "(?i)\\b(death|die|dies|died|dying|dead|grave)\\b")),
    Love = mean(str_detect(text, "(?i)\\b(love|loved|loves|lover)\\b")),
    Nature = mean(str_detect(text, "(?i)\\b(bee|bees|bird|birds|flower|flowers|sun|snow|wind)\\b")),
    God = mean(str_detect(text, "(?i)\\b(god|heaven|angel|angels|eternity)\\b"))
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "theme", values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(theme = fct_reorder(theme, share))

themes
```

```{r}
ggplot(themes, aes(x = share, y = theme)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Share of Poems Mentioning Each Theme",
    subtitle = "Based on keyword matches",
    x = "Percent of poems with at least one matching word",
    y = "Theme"
  )
```

**What the plot shows.** Each bar is the percent of poems that contain at least one word
from that theme, with the most common theme at the top. The most common theme is
**`r as.character(themes$theme[which.max(themes$share)])`**, which appears in
`r round(100 * max(themes$share))`% of the poems. The least common is
**`r as.character(themes$theme[which.min(themes$share)])`**, at
`r round(100 * min(themes$share))`%. This is a rough measure, because a poem can use the
word "grave" without being mainly about death.

## Question 2: Does the dashes differ across file groups?

```{r}
dash_by_group <- poems |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(avg_dashes = mean(n_dashes)) |>
  mutate(group = fct_reorder(group, avg_dashes))

dash_by_group
```

```{r}
ggplot(dash_by_group, aes(x = group, y = avg_dashes)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkorange") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Number of Dashes per Poem",
    subtitle = "Compared across the three file groups",
    x = "File group",
    y = "Average dashes per poem"
  )
```

**What the plot shows.** Each bar is the average number of dashes (`--`) per poem in one
file group, ordered from lowest to highest. The group with the most dashes is
**`r as.character(dash_by_group$group[which.max(dash_by_group$avg_dashes)])`**, at about
`r round(max(dash_by_group$avg_dashes), 1)` per poem. The group with the fewest is
**`r as.character(dash_by_group$group[which.min(dash_by_group$avg_dashes)])`**, at about
`r round(min(dash_by_group$avg_dashes), 1)`. If the bars are close, the dash is a steady
habit across her poems, and if they differ a lot, the groups are quite different in style.

## Conclusion

Her poems return to a few big themes, and the dash is a regular part of her style. A
limitation is that my keyword lists were chosen by hand, so they miss words I
didn't think of. The text for each poem also includes its title and number, which might
add extra matches.
